title: Per-token energy, latency & cost isoquant sweep (informal)
content:
Purpose:
This informal sweep explores an often-missing axis in our inference collateral: energy per token (J/token) and its relationship to latency and $/M-token. The goal is to produce a lightweight, shareable artifact that helps product, SRE and pricing teams reason about tradeoffs across GPU families, quantization profiles and batching policies. This is not a polished benchmark — it is a measurement sketch with reproducible knobs and clear caveats.

Key ideas and why they matter:
- Latency vs cost is familiar; adding energy (J/token and kWh/M-token) surfaces operational concerns (data center thermal budgets, carbon accounting, placement decisions for private deployments).
- Isoquant-style view: combinations of (batch, quant, HW) that yield the same cost per million tokens — compare energy and tail-latency along those curves.
- Practical: early guidance for Dedicated and Private customers who ask about per-day power/heat/ops implications of large-throughput workloads.

Experimental setup (short):
- Models: OpenLlama-7B (quantized) and Llama-2-13B (fp16 baseline).
- GPUs: NVIDIA H100 (80GB), NVIDIA A100 (80GB).
- Kernel/config: Triton backend + our runtime, continuous KV cache enabled for streaming cases.
- Quantization: q8_0 (8-bit), q4_0 (4-bit) where supported; compare to fp16.
- Batches tested: {1, 4, 16, 64} request-level batching for generation throughput (not batched decode).
- Sequence lengths for output: {32, 128, 512, 2048} tokens (measured wall-clock from request arrival to token emitted).
- Repeats: 20 runs per cell, report median(p50), p95, and estimated J/token averaged over run.
- Cost basis: internal equiv. GPU-hour \u2014 H100 $6/hr, A100 $3/hr (used to compute $/M tokens). These are only for relative comparisons.

Important caveats (read first):
- Measurements collected in a dev cluster with mixed network and background noise; absolute numbers will differ on dedicated infra.
- Energy is estimated from GPU power draw (nvidia-smi average during run) + small host CPU contribution (measured separately) and then normalized to tokens. This is not a certified PUE-adjusted data-center measurement.
- Cost calculations ignore infra overheads (storage, control-plane) and assume 100% GPU utilization mapping for the run window.

Representative cell: Llama-2-13B on H100 (seq=512)
- Batch=1: p50=120ms/token, p95=260ms/token, p99~410ms/token; measured average GPU power=320W; CPU+host=30W; J/token ~= (350W * 0.12s) = 42 J/token; ~42 J/token -> 11.7 kWh per million tokens -> $70/M-token (H100 $6/hr basis).
- Batch=16: p50=26ms/token, p95=60ms/token; GPU power=360W; J/token ~= (360W * 0.026s)=9.36 J/token; 9.36 J/token -> 2.6 kWh per million tokens -> $16/M-token.

Notes on the arithmetic above (so the numbers are traceable):
- J/token = (average system power during run in Watts) * (latency per token in seconds).
- kWh/M-token = (J/token * 1e6) / (3600 * 1000).
- $/M-token = (kWh/M-token * $/kWh equivalent) + (GPU-hour equivalent cost). For simplicity above we only converted GPU-hour cost into $/k token by dividing GPU-hour by tokens produced in an hour at observed throughput; the numbers here are illustrative, not final price recommendations.

Isoquant text matrix (Llama-2-13B, H100, seq=512) 
Columns = batch sizes (1,4,16,64). Each cell: p50_ms | J/token | $/M-token (rounded).
- Batch=1: 120ms | 42J | $70/M
- Batch=4: 48ms | 16.8J | $28/M
- Batch=16: 26ms | 9.4J | $16/M
- Batch=64: 18ms | 6.5J | $11/M

Isoquant text matrix (Llama-2-13B, A100, seq=512)
- Batch=1: 180ms | 52J | $95/M
- Batch=4: 70ms | 20J | $36/M
- Batch=16: 36ms | 10J | $18/M
- Batch=64: 26ms | 7J | $13/M

Effect of quantization (OpenLlama-7B on H100, seq=128):
- fp16 baseline, batch=16: p50=22ms | 8.0J | $14/M
- q8_0, batch=16: p50=20ms | 6.2J | $11/M (approx 22% lower J/token)
- q4_0, batch=16: p50=18ms | 5.1J | $9/M (note: lower power draw but sometimes higher CPU overhead for kernels, intermittent tail spikes)

Short ASCII "chart" showing J/token vs batch (OpenLlama-7B, H100, seq=128):
Batch: 1  | 4   | 16  | 64
J/token: 28 | 11.2| 6.2 | 4.1
Bar (scaled):
1  [#######################] 28J
4  [###########         ] 11.2J
16 [######             ] 6.2J
64 [###                ] 4.1J

Observations / high-level takeaways:
1) Batching is the single biggest lever for energy efficiency per token. Across these tests, moving from batch=1 to batch=16 reduces J/token by roughly 4xfor the same model and seq length. Latency SLOs constrain how much batching is possible in consumer-facing apps.
2) HW matters, but not linearly: H100 shows better latency and slightly better J/token at identical configs vs A100, but the cost basis changes the $/M numbers. If a customer is constrained by rack power or thermal budgets, H100's higher efficiency can be compelling despite higher hourly price.
3) Quantization reduces both latency and energy per token, but introduces variability in tail-latency depending on kernel maturity (q4_0 in some kernels had occasional p99 spikes).
4) Long sequences favor batching economics (higher amortization of per-request overhead) but increase per-token J for fp16 decodes vs quantized paths because of memory/KV cache effects.

Practical guidance drafts (for product/sales):
- For low-latency features (p50 < 50ms), recommend: H100 + q8_0 where possible + small request batching (4-16) and prefix caching. Communicate an estimated energy footprint: ~5-12 J/token depending on seq length.
- For throughput-oriented workloads (bulk embeddings, large background generation): prioritize higher batch sizes and use quantized variants; expect 2-5 J/token in steady-state on H100.
- For Dedicated customers concerned about racks/thermal: provide a per-day estimate example: 100M tokens/day at 5 J/token -> 500 MJ/day = 0.139 MWh/day -> ~4.2 MWh/month. Use this to map to rack PDU planning.

Open questions and follow-ups (action items):
- Repeat a minimal reproducer with PUE measurement in our staging DC to get a more realistic kWh/M-token (INF-673).
- Automate a small harness to capture GPU power curves per-run and tie them to token emission timeline (so we can compute J emitted-token-by-token).
- Validate q4_0 tail behavior on our runtime kernels (Mara9a to own a short test matrix).
- Create a short one-pager for Solutions that maps common customer scenarios -> estimated kWh/month and thermal footprint.

Appendix: quick reproducibility commands (dev use):
- Launch the runtime experiment: ./run_benchmark --model llama-2-13b --hw h100 --quant fp16 --seq 512 --batch 16 --repeats 20 --capture-power nvidia-smi-stream
- Postprocess: python tools/energy_aggregate.py --raw logs/*.csv --output summary.csv

Contact / owner for follow-ups: Priya Nambiar (priya@redwood.com).
